The negative absolute temperature is an interesting concept to see where our current mathematical models bring us when applied to rather unconventional systems. I hesitate to call it temperature by the way, because originally, temperature is supposed to be a measure of the following: You have a system in a certain thermodynamic state. You bring it in contact with an ideal gas. The two equilibrate (system+gas). You can measure the temperature of the gas by measuring its kinetic energy state, from which you can determine the temperature of the system.

This means that temperature is technically only defined for an open system. But only a closed system can be at a negative temperature. Once you bring it into contact with something else, it will have a (very high) positive temperature. The math works out, and these population-inverted systems do have interesting properties and applications (a laser needs a population inversion to work). The most important result from this has actually been a renewed interest in the postulates and mathematical machinery upon which thermodynamics is founded. Two competing definitions for entropy that were thought to be 100% equivalent are now known to result in differing predictions for the temperature of these closed population-inverted systems.

In other words, they've used maths to quantify the steps of cooling, allowing researchers to define set speed limit for how cold a system can get in a finite amount of time.
